text.p: House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich, seeking to defend his role as Republican leader, said on Saturday that admitting to ethics violations was the "most honourable thing to do" to resolve the two-year investigation.

In his first public comments on his unprecedented ethics headaches, Gingrich said he was the victim of a House double standard in judging ethics cases and that Democrats including minority leader Representative Richard Gephardt had run into problems but been let off lightly.
He also noted that a number of tax-exempt organisations were able to keep their status despite political objectives, singling out the Sierra Club which has as one of its goals Gingrich's defeat.
Speaking at a packed town meeting in his home district, the Georgia Republican said he had trusted his lawyers to guide him through the complex congressionial code of conduct.

"I trusted the law firm to have done the job right. They didn't do the job right and I didn't catch them, so I thought the most honourable thing to do when you have done something wrong is to say, 'This was a mistake,'" he said.
"Saying upfront, this was a mistake, is the only honourable thing you can do if you've made a mistake," he said.
Gingrich's self-defence was prompted by a question from a teenage girl, who wondered how it was possible for him to continue as speaker after having "disgraced" the House.

Gingrich said the media was partly responsible for his ethics troubles, and accused Democrats of trying to keep public attention on his unprecedented reprimand and $300,000 penalty in order to avoid talking about the "things that really matter," namely the Republican legislative agenda.
"The No. 1 focus we have for the next five weeks is to pass the constitutional amendment to require a balanced budget," Gingrich said to applause from about 500 supporters.
Gingrich staff distributed handouts on the ethics issue, which the speaker said would avoid "a whole new wave of controversy, which is the thing that our opponents would most like."

The handouts were three Jan. 17 memos that Ohio Republican Representative John Boehner, a staunch Gingrich ally, provided for House Republicans as part of a coordinated counterattack against adverse publicity from the speaker's ethics case.

The documents said Gingrich was not found in violation of U.S. tax laws by the House ethics panel, claimed the speaker's missteps had been nothing as serious as the scandals that have rocked the White House and warned readers to expect "hot rhetoric and gross exaggeration" from the speaker's opponents.

The meeting came as the 53-year-old conservative and his allies struggled to weather a storm of controversy in Washington raised by a scathing House Ethics Committee report and Tuesday's 395-28 vote to reprimand him and impose a $300,000 penalty.

Under an effective plea-bargain arrangement, the committee made no finding as to whether Gingrich used tax-exempt funds illegally for partisan political purposes in the form of his college course, entitled "Renewing American Civilisation." But the former history professor admitted he should have sought legal advice on the question.

The biggest task now before Gingrich was to find a way to pay his six-figure penalty that would not arouse a new furore as the House began a new session. Many members of Congress have said Gingrich should not take the money from his campaign warchest.

The speaker already has turned away at least $300,000 in voluntary pledges from callers around the country, according to his staff. Such donations would be considered campaign funds under U.S. election law.
